analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies and wholesalers import cheaper FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 57 cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to a House committee and died in a subcommittee when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal law so that licensed American pharmacists and wholesalers could buy prescription drugs from Canada, where the same FDA-approved medicines often sell for far less. It would also have made it illegal for drug manufacturers to punish or cut off pharmacists who bought drugs abroad, and would have let individuals import up to a 90-day personal supply from Canada. It included testing, documentation, and registration requirements meant to keep counterfeit drugs out. The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and no vote was ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially seniors and people without drug coverage, who could buy the same medicines at Canadian prices. Pharmacies and wholesalers also gain a new, legal supply channel.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write regulations allowing pharmacists and wholesalers to import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada into the United States.

Prohibits drug manufacturers from discriminating against U.S. pharmacists or wholesalers — for example, by giving foreign buyers better terms or restricting their supply of drugs that are legal to import.
Requires the Secretary to grant individuals a waiver to import a personal 90-day supply of an FDA-approved drug from a registered Canadian pharmacy with a valid prescription.

Requires built-in safeguards — batch testing for authenticity, detailed documentation, registration of foreign sellers, and suspension of importers found shipping counterfeit products — and orders independent studies of importer compliance and of the effect on retail drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose some ability to charge Americans higher prices than buyers in other countries pay for the same drugs. Federal regulators would also bear the cost of writing and enforcing importation rules.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of drug importation have long argued that medicines bought abroad carry a higher risk of counterfeit, misbranded, or degraded products reaching patients; this bill tries to answer that with mandatory batch testing and documentation, but critics say no testing regime fully removes the risk.

The new protections depend on the Secretary of Health and Human Services writing detailed regulations and enforcing them, so the actual level of safety and access would hinge on how a future administration implemented the law.

Large-scale importation from a country with Canada's population could strain the Canadian drug supply and push Canadian prices up, an objection raised repeatedly in the importation debates of this era.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for patients is large: identical FDA-approved drugs often cost substantially less in Canada, and this bill would have opened a legal, regulated channel to buy them, with anti-retaliation rules to keep manufacturers from cutting off importers. The main cost is the safety-enforcement burden and a residual counterfeit-drug risk that testing requirements reduce but cannot eliminate. On balance, a bill with this many built-in safeguards was a serious, good-faith attempt, and its death without a vote meant patients never saw the savings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2005 without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders of Vermont introduced the Prescription Drug Parity for Americans Act on June 17, 2003.
It gathered 57 cosponsors — 55 Democrats and 2 Republicans — including original cosponsors Sherrod Brown, Ron Paul, John Murtha, and Barney Frank.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and a week later to the committee's Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a markup or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: they continued selling at U.S. prices without Canadian importation undercutting them, and they never had to face a vote on the anti-discrimination provisions. Patients paying U.S. prices gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers, whose prices were protected

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to legalize prescription drug importation from Canada.

for.name: 55 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up 55 of its 57 cosponsors.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to the Health Subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or a vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
against.what_they_did: Fought drug importation legislation throughout this era, arguing it would endanger patients and undermine drug innovation.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 55 of the 57 cosponsors were Democrats, with only 2 Republicans — and the Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: Importation from Canada would have let American pharmacies buy the same FDA-approved drugs at the lower prices charged abroad, shrinking the higher U.S. prices manufacturers depend on. The bill's anti-discrimination provision would have barred them from cutting off or penalizing importers, so they fought importation bills throughout this period.

The bill makes pharmacists and wholesalers the legal importers of Canadian drugs and forbids manufacturers from discriminating against them for buying abroad. Their gain comes from a cheaper supply they can pass to patients.
Licensed Canadian sellers would register with the FDA and become a supply channel for American importers and individual 90-day personal-use purchases.
